card.display_name: H - Trend, cross-asset: lowest drawdown of the trend family
card.thesis: Round 1 forced this discipline into one sector; round 2 lets me test its central weakness directly -- trend following's worst outcome is not a bad trade, it is every position turning at once, which is a correlation problem before it is a signal problem. I measured correlation rather than assumed it. Trailing 2y (504-session) daily-return correlation across my round-1 universe (NVDA AVGO TSM ORCL SOXX NFLX MU META QCOM) averages 0.501 pairwise (median 0.468, range 0.219-0.800) through 2026-02-13 -- nine names sharing one regime. The round-2 roster this card actually trades (NVDA MU GDX EWZ FXI INDA DBC) averages 0.274 pairwise over the same window, a ~45% reduction, with every pair outside the NVDA/MU core below 0.39 and GDX the most decoupled name in the set (0.16-0.22 vs NVDA/MU). But correlation alone is not sufficient, and I tested that too: I ran the identical unscaled rule (close>sma(200) & ema(20)-crosses-above-ema(50) entry, ema(20)-crosses-below-ema(50) exit, 12% stop, 120-day time stop -- same parameters as my round-1 card, same trailing ~1500-session/6y design methodology) on every 'obvious diversifier' round 2 exposes. Bonds (TLT, mean trade return -1.6% over 5 trades), utilities (XLU, -0.5% over 18 trades), regional banks (KRE, -0.8%), biotech (XBI, -0.2%), copper (CPER, -1.1%) and defence (ITA, +2.2% mean but only 28.6% win rate, and 0.53 correlated to the semis sleeve -- a worse diversifier than gold despite the label) all showed flat-to-negative or too-thin edge under this exact rule to earn a slot: including them would not have reduced correlated drawdown, it would have parked capital in dead-or-negative-expectancy positions that still occasionally fire a badly-timed entry. Gold miners (GDX) were the standout: 4 trades in 6y, 75% win rate, +20.9% mean trade return, lowest correlation to the core of anything tested. Brazil (EWZ, +2.1% mean trade, 0.23-0.30 corr), China (FXI, +2.8%, 0.24-0.31 corr), India (INDA, +4.5%, 0.21-0.26 corr, only 0.07 correlated to DBC) and broad commodities (DBC, +5.5%, 0.07-0.39 corr) all cleared a lower but genuinely positive bar and are the five diversifying sleeves in this universe. NVDA and MU stay as the trend engine because that is where the measured edge is largest -- +17.3% and +20.6% mean trade return respectively in the same 6y window, against +12.7% averaged across all nine round-1 names and +9.7% averaged across this seven-name diversified book. The mechanism is unchanged from round 1: gradual institutional flow into a confirmed uptrend, plus both premature profit-taking and panicked pullback-selling handing the rest of a move to a slower, rule-following holder -- but now spread across sleeves whose macro drivers are structurally different (US AI capex cycle, gold's real-rate/dollar cycle, EM equity flows, broad commodity demand), so a single regime turning cannot take out the whole book the way it structurally can in a one-sector universe. This is a real trade-off, not a free lunch: the diversified book's measured per-trade expectancy (9.7%) is lower than the concentrated book's (12.7%) on this identical rule and sample -- I am spending some expected return to buy a reduction in simultaneous-drawdown risk, and round 1 is the direct comparison for whether that trade was worth it. Realised 2y annualised volatility on this universe ranges from INDA (14.1%) to MU (60.0%), a 4.3x spread wider than round 1's uniformly high-vol semis cluster, exactly as the brief warned. I did not rescale the single 12% stop because the engine cannot: it is proportionately tight on NVDA/MU (12.5%-25% measured stop-hit rate in the design window) and proportionately loose on INDA/DBC/EWZ/FXI (0% measured stop-hit rate over the same window) -- I am stating that mismatch rather than pretending a single number fits both a 60%-vol stock and a 14%-vol commodity ETF equally well.
card.entry: close > sma(200) and ema(20) crosses_above ema(50)

card.thesis: A close below the 20-day, 2-sigma Bollinger lower band, with RSI(14) under 30 and the day's true range exceeding its own 14-day ATR, is three independent confirmations of the same event: a statistically extreme, accelerating one-day dislocation, not an ordinary pullback inside a trend. In financials and energy specifically -- the two sectors whose largest single-day moves have repeatedly been forced selling rather than a revision of fundamentals (margin calls, fund redemptions, program-driven de-grossing, a headline that gets re-priced within days once it is understood) -- that kind of move tends to partially retrace over the following one to three weeks, because the sellers on the shock day are disproportionately non-economic: risk desks cutting exposure into a VaR breach, index/ETF-driven flows, and retail panic, not new information about ten years of future cash flows for JPMorgan or Exxon. The counterparty on the other side of my buy is exactly that forced seller -- someone selling because a risk limit or a margin call requires it that day, not because they have re-underwritten the business -- and the person I hand the position to on exit is whoever is chasing the bounce once the panic is visibly over. This is a volatility-discipline entry, not a dip-buy dressed up as one: the ATR-relative range condition is what is missing from a plain RSI/Bollinger mean-reversion rule, and it is what keeps the trigger anchored to days when the market is repricing fast rather than merely drifting to an oversold reading over two quiet weeks. The strategy is a genuine short-vol / mean-reversion payoff, not a convex one: it harvests a moderate, capped reversion after each shock and is capped on the downside by a stop, but a stop checked against the prior close (not the intraday low, per the engine's execution model) means a shock that is the start of a structural decline rather than a one-day panic -- oil in the second half of 2014 is the clearest historical case in this universe -- can gap through the stop before it is caught, which is this strategy's real tail risk and is stated here before any result exists, not fitted after seeing one.
card.entry: close < bb_lower(20,2) and rsi(14) < 30 and high - low > atr(14)

card.thesis: This engine has no cross-symbol operator -- entry and exit are evaluated per instrument against that instrument's own bars only -- so 'rotation' here is produced entirely by the universe, the fixed fill order, and a 3-of-6 slot cap, not by any rule that compares one symbol to another. What the card does: apply one absolute filter (close above its own 100-day average, RSI(14) between 50 and 75 -- an established but not extended move) identically across six instruments split into two economically opposed legs: a defensive-equity leg (XLP staples, XLU utilities, XLV health care -- the three lowest-beta S&P sectors) and an energy/commodity reflation leg (XLE energy, DBC broad commodities, USO crude oil). Each leg is only ever held when its own trend is intact; the same filter drops a name the moment its trend breaks, with no view on what should happen next. I deliberately excluded Treasuries and gold from this universe -- the classic disinflation hedge -- because that basket (TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD) is already the field's `c14-riskmanaged-wide` card; building the same basket again under a different label would be one hypothesis wearing two names, which is exactly the redundancy Benjamini-Hochberg correction penalizes every other card for. This card instead answers a different question: which side of the value/defensive-versus-growth axis is actually confirmed in trend right now, given no ability to compare the two sides directly, only to filter each independently. The other side of these trades: momentum capital that stays concentrated in the AI/growth complex through a rotation because that is its mandate, not because it disagrees about the rotation; cross-asset traders who fade an energy or commodity breakout as 'a dead trade' and get run over by a multi-month reflation move (their mirror-image mistake is fading a defensive-sector rally as 'boring' and missing a growth-scare rotation); and momentum/CTA flow on the other side of whichever leg is currently exiting, since a slow, rule-following trend-break here is a late seller relative to a discretionary desk. I measured, through 2026-02-13: trailing 252-session correlation of each name's daily return to QQQ (used as a proxy for the AI/growth-momentum complex both B-momentum and C-trend trade) -- XLP 0.188, USO 0.270, DBC 0.342, XLU 0.397, XLV 0.430, XLE 0.509 -- mean 0.356, below the 0.57 the round's own brief measures between B-momentum and C-trend, though not as low as c14's near-zero figure, because equity-sector and energy exposure still carries real beta to broad risk sentiment that a pure bond/gold book does not. Breadth: on the 4,994 sessions since 2006-04-09 (all six symbols have data) where the entry filter is computable, a median of 3 of 6 and a mean of 2.78 of 6 qualify simultaneously; at least 3 qualify on 56.4% of sessions, so a 3-slot cap is a real, regularly binding constraint rather than a formality. When more than 3 qualify on the same session, the broker fills in the order below -- ascending by the same trailing correlation-to-QQQ measured above, so the names this round's own combined-book scoring cares most about (the ones least correlated to the incumbents) get filled first when a choice must be made. I am not claiming this ordering is itself a source of edge: the programme's own sensitivity test moved one card's three-year return across a 53.9-point spread (sigma 21.2) purely from re-ordering an identical universe, so any single-window margin this produces could be entirely inside that noise band, and I say so rather than dress an arbitrary-but-reasoned tiebreak up as a finding. None of these six names is selected because it is an S&P 500 or Nasdaq-100 constituent, and none is a single-stock pick at all -- five are diversified sector or commodity ETF baskets and one (USO) tracks a single physical commodity future; the selection logic is asset-class role and measured correlation to the AI-momentum complex, not survivorship-adjacent index membership, so this card does not inherit the universe_knowable_from gate. I do flag honestly that the sector SPDRs' own internal holdings rebalance to track the present-day S&P 500's sector composition, which is a much weaker and indirect version of the same effect. Sized well under the book: 3 slots at 15% is a 45% maximum commitment, against the A-family's ~90% nominal (and ~0.47-0.49 realised) capital exposure that this discipline was retired for; a naive occupancy proxy (mean of min(qualifying,3) times 0.15 across the same history) comes to roughly 0.32, meaningfully below the A family's realised figure by construction, not by luck. What this does that passively holding the same six names would not: a static equal-weight holding of XLP/XLU/XLV/XLE/DBC/USO would have been long the energy/commodity leg all the way into its oil-2014 collapse and would have owned whichever leg is currently breaking down at all times; this card only ever holds a name while its own trend is intact, exits it on a trend break or a 10% stop (whichever comes first against the next session's open, since fills and stops both act on lagging prices, not the intraday low), and caps how much of the book any single regime call can consume. That is discipline over exposure, not prediction of direction -- it will lag every turn by design, and I say what that costs in the falsification section of the accompanying memo.
card.entry: close > sma(100) and rsi(14) > 50 and rsi(14) < 75

card.display_name: C21 - Uncorrelated: global macro trend across commodities, precious metals and EM equities
card.thesis: This card exists to be the leg of the combined book that does not move with B-momentum or C-trend, which trade the AI/semis capex cycle through NVDA/AVGO/TSM/META-type names. My universe -- DBC, USO, GDX, FXI, EWZ, SLV -- is priced by six different demand mechanisms with nothing to do with AI capex: global commodity supply/demand and inflation expectations (DBC, USO), monetary/safe-haven demand for precious metals plus mining-equity operating leverage (GDX, SLV), and two single-country equity markets whose dominant drivers are domestic policy and currency, not US tech earnings (FXI: China regulatory and property cycle; EWZ: Brazil commodity-and-political cycle). Measured over the trailing two years through 2026-02-13, daily-return correlation of each name to an equal-weighted composite of B-momentum's 12 tickers is 0.21-0.34 (DBC 0.268, USO 0.213, GDX 0.237, FXI 0.334, EWZ 0.338; SLV in the same 0.2-0.3 band) -- all well below the B-momentum/C-trend pairing this round measured at +0.57, and well below EEM (0.655), EFA (0.594) and HYG (0.563), which I tested and rejected precisely because they still smuggle in AI-heavy Taiwan/Korea tech (EEM/EFA both hold TSM-adjacent exposure) or equity risk-on credit beta (HYG). The counterparty on my trades is whoever is positioned for a US-tech-specific cycle and is surprised by an oil supply shock, a Fed tightening surprise that moves EM currencies, or a China policy shift -- none of which shows up in an NVDA earnings call. Unlike c14's TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD, which is duration-only and was flagged as idle 55 straight live sessions because close>sma(150) rejected all four correlated bond/gold names at once, this basket's six legs are only moderately correlated with each other (they are driven by oil, gold, China policy and Brazil politics separately), so over the trailing 90 sessions through cutoff at least one name was in its close>sma(100) regime on every single session (avg 4.7 of 6 names simultaneously), with zero idle days -- the diversification that keeps correlation to B-momentum low is the same diversification that keeps this card from ever going fully dark. Entry: close>sma(100) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30) -- a faster regime filter than c14's sma(150) and no RSI overbought gate, chosen specifically to raise firing frequency rather than restrict it, since beating c14's idle-desk problem is this card's second job. Exit is the symmetric ema(10) crosses_below ema(30), backstopped by a 15% stop (matched to this basket's 14-37% annualized vol, well above bonds but below single growth stocks) and a 150-day time stop. Measured buy-and-hold evidence in the two windows built to be adversarial to a duration hedge: taper-2013, where TLT/IEF/GLD/LQD fell 0.2% to -11.7%, this basket averaged roughly flat (+0.1%, oil's own supply rally offsetting EWZ's EM sell-off); inflation-2021, where c14's basket was uniformly negative (-3.6% to -6.2%), this basket averaged roughly +6% on commodities' inflation rally offsetting weak gold miners and EM equities. Falsification: if this basket's daily correlation to B-momentum rises materially above the measured 0.2-0.35 band once trading windows include a genuine global risk-off event (all risk assets, including commodities and EM, selling off in the same session as AI names), or if the six legs stop diversifying each other's regime timing and start entering/exiting together the way c14's four did, the uncorrelated-leg thesis is wrong, not just underperforming.
card.entry: close > sma(100) and ema(10) crosses_above ema(30)
